options: A CSV file in the seeds/ folder that dbt seed loads into the warehouse as a table
A Python script that generates synthetic test data
A type of dbt test that checks row counts
A live connection to an external API
questions.explain: A seed is just a CSV file, committed to the dbt project, that the dbt seed command loads into the warehouse as a real table.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what specific kind of data belongs in a seed?
options: Small, static reference data that doesn't come from a real source system, like a country-code lookup
Large fact tables with millions of rows
Any data at all, regardless of size or ownership
Frequently changing transactional data owned by an app database
questions.explain: Seeds exist for small, static, nobody-else-owns-it reference data — not for large or frequently changing data, which belongs in a real ingested source instead.

questions.q: Why might a seed's inferred column type need to be overridden with +column_types?
options: Because +column_types is required for every seed with no exceptions
Because CSV files don't support columns
Because inference can get ambiguous columns wrong, like values with leading zeros or currency-looking strings
Because dbt seed cannot infer any column types at all
questions.explain: dbt infers seed column types from the data, and ambiguous values (leading zeros, currency-like strings) are exactly where that inference gets it wrong — +column_types pins the type explicitly.

questions.q: How does a model reference a loaded seed?
options: By hardcoding the schema and table name directly
A special seed() function that only works on CSVs
Seeds cannot be referenced from models at all
The same ref() function used for any other model, e.g. ref('country_codes')
questions.explain: Once loaded, a seed is ref()-able exactly like any model — downstream SQL doesn't need to know it started life as a CSV.

questions.q: What is the sign that data should be a real source instead of a seed?
options: The seed table has a primary key
The seed was created more than a month ago
You find yourself editing the CSV every week
The CSV file is under 10 rows
questions.explain: A seed you're editing every week is a sign the data changes too often (or is owned by another system) to be a hand-typed CSV — it belongs in a real ingested source instead.
